title: On-demand billing for Fabric Data Warehouse (Preview)
author: Sosivara_msft

content.text:
Only pay for what you consume
Many warehouse workloads are highly variable. In some cases, a few peak periods demand significant compute, while the rest of the month usage is much lower. Shared capacity is a great fit for steady, predictable workloads, while workloads with variable or intermittent demand can benefit from a consumption-based model. On-demand billing for Fabric Data Warehouse gives you that flexibility: you can use dedicated compute when your warehouse needs it and pay for the compute you consume.
As introduced in the Fabric on-demand billing platform blog post this new billing model applies more broadly across Fabric. In this post, we'll go deeper on what it means specifically for Fabric Data Warehouse, including when to use it, how it works, and how to get started.
What's different
With on-demand billing in Fabric Data Warehouse:
• Isolate Data Warehouse compute from other Fabric workloads to avoid noisy neighbor problems
• Right-size compute independently for each workspace.
• Pay for the compute your warehouse consumes
• Get predictable behavior at the workspace ceiling, with queries queued instead of throttled
On-demand isn't a rip-and-replace; it's designed for warehouse workloads that benefit from consumption-based compute. You can use on demand for Data Warehouse while continuing to use shared capacity for other Fabric workloads, allowing you to choose the model that best fits each workload.
One thing worth stressing: on-demand billing introduces a new billing construct for Data Warehouse. It doesn't change how compute is provisioned, the backend architecture, or how users interact with the warehouse. What changes is how warehouse compute consumption is billed and controlled.
Two capacity models, one platform
Shared capacity and on demand complement each other. The right model depends on the workload scenario:
Shared capacity
On-demand billing
Best for
Steady, predictable workloads
Variable, bursty, or intermittent warehouse workloads
Example Scenarios
Dashboards, pipelines, and warehouse workloads with consistent demand
Month-end processing without sizing for peak demand throughout the month, intermittent development/test workloads without sizing for peak, or bursty production warehouse workloads that benefit from isolation
You pay for
Provisioned capacity
Compute consumed by warehouse
Isolation
All workloads share the same capacity
Warehouse compute is isolated from other Fabric workloads
Guardrails
Capacity SKU size
24-hour compute limit + workspace ceiling
For example, you can keep Power BI and pipelines on shared capacity while moving a warehouse with highly variable demand to on-demand billing. This lets you choose the billing model that best fits each workload.
What changes when you turn it on
When a capacity admin enables on-demand billing for Data Warehouse, every workspace in the capacity with a warehouse or SQL analytics endpoint begins consuming compute separately from the base capacity. Warehouse consumption also shows up as its own line item on your Azure bill, so capacity admins stop asking, "What was that F256 spike?" and start reading a bill that maps to actual work.
Control how much compute each workspace can use
On-demand billing gives administrators control over the maximum compute available to each workspace through a workspace compute ceiling. This lets you right-size compute for each workspace based on its workload requirements.
A useful mental model is to think of it like a road trip: your workspace compute ceiling is how fast you can drive. Set a higher ceiling when a workspace needs more compute for peak demand, or a lower ceiling when its requirements are more predictable.
Unlike a car, setting a higher ceiling doesn't mean you pay for it continuously. You pay for the compute you actually consume, not for the ceiling you've configured. This means you can set the ceiling high enough to accommodate peak bursts without paying for that maximum continuously. For additional cost control, administrators can also configure a spend limit that limits overall consumption within a 24-hour period.
The following illustration shows how to configure on-demand billing 24-hour compute limit and workspace compute ceilings for Data Warehouse.
Figure: Configuring on-demand 24-hour compute limit and workspace compute ceilings for Data Warehouse.
Give every team a lane
Workspace ceilings turn a single Fabric capacity into a multi-tenant compute environment for the warehouse. For example, your admin can assign the finance team a 256 CU lane for month-end close; the marketing team a 128 CU lane for segmentation; and the data science team a 512 CU burst lane for ad-hoc modeling. They all run on the same on-demand meter, but nobody's month-end close slows down because marketing kicked off a segmentation query. This provides predictable isolation between teams.
How it behaves in practice
When you use on-demand billing, Fabric automatically manages several aspects of workspace compute and query execution:
• Sensible defaults out of the box. Each workspace starts with a smart compute ceiling that mirrors the throughput you'd get with bursting on shared capacity. Admins can tune it per workspace later if needed.
• No throttling at the workspace ceiling. Queries that don't fit shrink-fit first, get queued, and only return an error if a single query needs more than the entire ceiling.
• GPU query acceleration is supported. Give acceleration-heavy workspaces a higher ceiling so they aren't throttled before they benefit.
• Custom SQL pools work as-is. The workspace ceiling becomes the pool able compute; the system pool auto-reserves ~⅓ and you allocate the rest.
Monitoring what's actually happening
On-demand billing consumption shows up in the Fabric Capacity Metrics app on a dedicated tab, alongside every other billing category on the capacity. Because there's no 24-hour smoothing on this tab, the graphs reflect real peaks and scaling activity that is useful for setting the right workspace ceiling and spend limit for the capacity.
The following query shows whether a pool is running on shared capacity or on-demand billing, based on `current_workspace_capacity` column in `sql_pool_insights` view.
SELECT
sql_pool_name,
current_workspace_capacity,
is_pool_under_pressure,
timestamp
FROM [your-warehouse-name].[queryinsights].[sql_pool_insights]
ORDER BY timestamp DESC;
How to estimate your on-demand bill (quick method)
Start with your previous month’s Data Warehouse spend on shared capacity and apply the on-demand multiplier:
• Estimated Data Warehouse on-demand cost ≈ last month Data Warehouse cost (from Azure bill) × 1.3.
• Estimated total cost ≈ shared-capacity cost for non-Data Warehouse workloads + (1.3 × last month Data Warehouse cost).
Getting started
If you're a capacity admin on a Fabric capacity with an eligible subscription:
• Open the Fabric admin portal, go to Capacity settings, and select your capacity.
• In the On-demand billing section, enable Data Warehouse.
• Set a 24-hour compute limit that reflects your budget for the category.
• Set the default compute ceiling for new and migrated workspaces
• Adjust the ceiling on any existing workspaces based on requirements.
Detailed steps, including how to size a workspace ceiling and how to allocate custom SQL pools, are in the Fabric Data Warehouse on-demand billing configuration guide.
The one line to remember
On-demand billing gives warehouse teams dedicated compute without requiring additional capacity purchases. Start with a single warehouse workload, monitor consumption patterns, and adjust workspace ceilings as needed.
We'd love to hear how you're using it. Share your feedback and experiences in the Fabric Community forum.
Next steps
Ready to get started? Learn more about on-demand billing for Fabric Data Warehouse, then use the on-demand billing configuration guide to configure workspace ceilings and pools. For additional questions and scenarios, see the on-demand billing FAQ.
